claim: The Notch-Delta pathway is required to distinguish target from non-target muscles in C. elegans egg-laying circuit.
source: We found that the Notch-Delta pathway was required to distinguish target from non-target muscles.
evidence: Based on genetic screen results showing mutations in lin-12/Notch, apx-1/Delta, and sel-12/presenilin affect vm2 muscle arm development

claim: APX-1/Delta acts in surrounding cells including the non-target vm1 to activate LIN-12/Notch in the target vm2.
source: APX-1/Delta acts in surrounding cells including the non-target vm1 to activate LIN-12/Notch in the target vm2.
evidence: Cell-specific rescue experiments and expression pattern analysis showing apx-1 expression in vm1 and secondary vulval epithelial cells, and lin-12 expression in vm2

claim: LIN-12 functions cell-autonomously to up-regulate the expression of UNC-40/DCC and MADD-2 in vm2.
source: LIN-12 functions cell-autonomously to up-regulate the expression of UNC-40/DCC and MADD-2 in vm2, which in turn function together to promote muscle arm formation and guidance.
evidence: Mosaic analysis showing lin-12 rescue requires expression in vm2, and expression data showing UNC-40 and MADD-2 are down-regulated in lin-12 mutants

claim: UNC-40/DCC and MADD-2 function together to promote muscle arm formation and guidance.
source: LIN-12 functions cell-autonomously to up-regulate the expression of UNC-40/DCC and MADD-2 in vm2, which in turn function together to promote muscle arm formation and guidance.
evidence: Genetic analysis showing both unc-40 and madd-2 mutants have muscle arm defects, and double mutant analysis showing enhancement

claim: Ectopic expression of UNC-40/DCC in non-target vm1 muscle is sufficient to induce muscle arm extension from these cells.
source: Ectopic expression of UNC-40/DCC in non-target vm1 muscle is sufficient to induce muscle arm extension from these cells.
evidence: Experimental data showing that misexpression of UNC-40 in vm1 cells induces dendritic spine-like membrane extensions

claim: The LIN-12/Notch signaling specifies target selection by selectively up-regulating guidance molecules and forming muscle arms in target cells.
source: Therefore, the LIN-12/Notch signaling specifies target selection by selectively up-regulating guidance molecules and forming muscle arms in target cells.
evidence: Integration of genetic, expression, and rescue data showing the pathway from LIN-12 to UNC-40/MADD-2 to muscle arm formation

claim: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists of four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2).
source: The C. elegans egg-laying circuit consists four type 1 vulval muscle cells (vm1) and four type 2 vulval muscle cells (vm2), which form two X-shaped structures near the vulval opening
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge of C. elegans

claim: Egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2.
source: While vm1 and vm2 are from a common lineage, are physically adjacent and share many molecular components, the egg-laying motoneurons HSN and VC4/5 form serotoninergic and cholinergic chemical synapses exclusively on vm2
evidence: Based on prior EM reconstruction and neurotransmitter studies cited in the manuscript

claim: vm1 is mainly controlled by vm2 via gap junctions.
source: vm1 is mainly controlled by vm2 via gap junctions
evidence: Based on prior EM reconstruction work

claim: HSN presynaptic specializations are closely juxtaposed against the dendritic spine-like membrane protrusions (muscle arms) from the vm2 cell bodies.
source: Consistent with EM reconstruction, we found that the HSN presynaptic specializations were closely juxtaposed against the dendritic spine-like membrane protrusions (muscle arms) from the vm2 cell bodies when viewed from both the lateral and ventral sides
evidence: Fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1B confirming EM reconstruction

claim: UNC-103E is dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms.
source: low level of transgenic expression of UNC-103E::GFP with an integrated single-copy transgene showed that UNC-103E was dramatically enriched on vm2 muscle arms
evidence: Imaging data from single-copy transgene shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: HSN neurons are not required for vm2 specification and muscle arm development.
source: We therefore asked whether the HSN neurons are required for vm2 specification and muscle arm development by examining the vm2 morphology in the egl-1(n986) mutant, in which the HSN neurons undergo programmed cell death in embryonic stage. Surprisingly, in all of the examined animals, the morphology and position of vm2 muscle arms were indistinguishable from the wild type counterparts
evidence: Experimental data from egl-1 mutants shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Presynaptic components are dispensable for vm2 postsynaptic development.
source: These results indicate that presynaptic components are dispensable for vm2 postsynaptic development.
evidence: Based on experiments showing normal vm2 muscle arms in egl-1, egl-1;lin-39, and unc-104 mutants lacking presynaptic neurons or vesicles

claim: Vulval epithelial cells are required for normal vulval muscle differentiation and morphogenesis.
source: This result suggests that the vulval epithelial cells are required for normal vulval muscle differentiation and morphogenesis, and therefore might be also important for vm2 postsynaptic muscle arm development.
evidence: Observation of severe defects in lin-3 mutants which have abnormal vulval epithelial cell fate

claim: lin-12(wy750) mutant animals have completely absent vm2 muscle arm structures.
source: In lin-12(wy750) mutant animals, while the muscle morphology of both vm1 and vm2 were largely normal, the SER-1B::GFP labeled vm2 muscle arm structures were completely absent
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 1D,E,F

claim: lin-12(wy750) mutants have no vulval morphogenesis defects.
source: Surprisingly, we found no vulval morphogenesis defect in lin-12(wy750) mutants either by differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy or the localization pattern of the ajm-1::gfp apical junction marker at several development stages
evidence: DIC and fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A

claim: apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants show similar defective vm2 muscle arm development to lin-12(wy750).
source: Two other mutants isolated from the same screen, apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760), were very similar to the lin-12(wy750) mutant in their specific defective vm2 muscle arm development and normal vulval muscle development
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 1D

claim: lin-12(wy750) mutants lay notably fewer eggs compared to wild-type animals.
source: First, the muscle arm defective mutants laid notably fewer eggs compared to the wild-type animals
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 2A

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants retain eggs longer than wild-type animals.
source: Second, the muscle arm defective mutants retained eggs longer than the wild-type animals, as indicated by the higher percentage of late-stage embryos laid by the mutants
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 2B

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants have more frequent Ca2+ transients than wild type.
source: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had a twofold increase in the frequency of Ca2+ transient peaks
evidence: Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 2H

claim: lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants have significantly fewer synchronous double transients compared to wild type.
source: We also found that lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants had significantly fewer synchronous double transients compared to the wild type
evidence: Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 2I

claim: The average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients increased from ~100 ms in wild type to ~800 ms in lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants.
source: In wild-type animals, the average anterior/posterior delay was only ∼100 ms. In both lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants, the average anterior/posterior delay in double Ca2+ transients increased to ∼800 ms
evidence: Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 2J

claim: vm2 muscle arms are required for the synchronous excitation of anterior and posterior vulval muscles needed to successfully execute egg-laying behavior.
source: Together, these results show that the vm2 muscle arms lacking in lin-12(wy750) and apx-1(wy755) mutants are not necessary for excitation of the vulval muscles, but suggest they are required for the synchronous excitation of anterior and posterior vulval muscles needed to successfully execute egg-laying behavior.
evidence: Ca2+ imaging data showing asynchronous transients in mutants

claim: lin-12(wy750) contains a single missense mutation (G473R) in one of the conserved extracellular EGF domains of the LIN-12 protein.
source: Sequence analyses revealed that lin-12(wy750) contained a single missense mutation (G473R) in one of the conserved extracellular EGF domains of the LIN-12 protein
evidence: DNA sequencing data shown in Table 1

claim: lin-12(wy750) is a loss-of-function allele.
source: Two additional results indicated that lin-12(wy750) was a loss-of-function allele. First, trans-heterozygotes between lin-12(wy750) and a canonical loss-of-function allele lin-12(n676n930) presented similar muscle arm defects. Second, a lin-12 genomic fragment including 5 kb of upstream regulatory sequence and the entire coding region of lin-12 strongly rescued the muscle arm phenotype of lin-12(wy750) mutants
evidence: Genetic complementation test and rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4A

claim: lin-12(wy750) represents a partial loss-of-function allele.
source: Since strong loss-of-function alleles of lin-12, apx-1 and sel-12 cause lethality, dramatic vulval morphogenesis or general muscle morphology phenotypes, which are all absent in lin-12(wy750) mutant animals, it is likely that the missense mutation we isolated represents a partial loss-of-function allele.
evidence: Comparison with known strong loss-of-function alleles and observed phenotypes

claim: Muscle arm development requires a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events.
source: These data suggest that partial loss of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity spares vulval morphogenesis but specifically impairs vm2 specification and muscle arm development, and that muscle arm development might require a higher level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activity compared with earlier developmental events
evidence: Analysis of partial vs complete loss-of-function alleles and their differential effects on developmental processes

claim: LIN-12/Notch signaling is required at the L4 stage for vm2 muscle arm development.
source: More than 80% of the animals still showed defective muscle arms when shifted from 25°C to 15°C at mid-L4
evidence: Temperature shift experiments shown in Figure 3B

claim: lin-12 function in regulating postsynaptic muscle arm development is independent of other known roles of lin-12.
source: The upshift and downshift experiments together suggest a novel function of lin-12 at the L4 stage in regulating the postsynaptic muscle arm development and synaptic target choice. This lin-12 function is independent of other known roles of lin-12, all of which occur prior to early-L4 stage.
evidence: Temperature shift experiments showing late requirement for lin-12

claim: LIN-12/Notch signaling functions cell-autonomously in vm2 to regulate postsynaptic specification and muscle arm development.
source: LIN-12/Notch signaling functions cell-autonomously in vm2 to regulate postsynaptic specification and muscle arm development
evidence: Mosaic analysis showing rescue only when lin-12 is expressed in vm2

claim: Expression of lin-12 in vm2 is necessary and sufficient to rescue the vm2 muscle arm phenotype.
source: We found that the expression of lin-12 in vm2 was necessary and sufficient to rescue the vm2 muscle arm phenotype
evidence: Mosaic analysis data shown in Figure 4A,B,C

claim: APX-1 is expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells.
source: We found that APX-1 was expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells
evidence: Expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: apx-1 functions non-cell-autonomously to regulate vm2 muscle arm development.
source: We found that the expression of apx-1 in the secondary vulval epithelial cells or vm1 cells was sufficient to rescue the vm2 muscle arm phenotype in apx-1(wy755) mutants
evidence: Cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 4F

claim: sel-12 functions cell-autonomously in vm2 to regulate muscle arm development.
source: We found that expression of sel-12 in vulval muscle cells completely rescued the vm2 muscle arm phenotype of sel-12(wy760), consistent with the cell-autonomous requirement of LIN-12/Notch signaling in vm2
evidence: Cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 4F

claim: The canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is involved in vm2 muscle arm development by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.
source: Additionally, specific expression of a dominant-negative lag-1 construct in the vulval muscles phenocopied the muscle arm defects observed in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy750) and sel-12(wy760) mutants, suggesting that the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway is likely involved by controlling the transcription of downstream genes.
evidence: Dominant-negative LAG-1 expression data shown in Figure 4F

claim: hlh-29 expression is dramatically down-regulated in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy755) and sel-12(wy760) mutants.
source: Moreover, the expression of a hlh-29 transcription reporter (hlh-29::gfp), a known target gene of the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2, was also dramatically down-regulated in lin-12(wy750), apx-1(wy755) and sel-12(wy760) mutants
evidence: Expression analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: APX-1 expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells activates the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 to promote the formation of the postsynaptic muscle arms.
source: Together, these results strongly support the model that APX-1 expressed in the secondary vulval epithelial cells and vm1 cells activates the canonical LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2 to promote the formation of the postsynaptic muscle arms.
evidence: Integration of expression, rescue, and genetic data

claim: apx-1 unilaterally promotes lin-12 expression and activates the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2.
source: Compared with wild-type animals, apx-1(wy755) mutant animals showed significantly reduced expression of lin-12 in vm2 cells, whereas the lin-12 expression in vulval epithelial cells was not affected. On the other hand, we did not observe any change of apx-1 expression in the lin-12(wy750) mutant. These results argue that apx-1 unilaterally promotes lin-12 expression and activates the LIN-12/Notch pathway in vm2.
evidence: Expression analysis shown in Figure 5B,C,D

claim: Three LAG-1 consensus binding sites exist in the promoter region of lin-12.
source: Indeed, we found three LAG-1 consensus binding sites in the promoter region of lin-12
evidence: Sequence analysis of lin-12 promoter

claim: lin-12(e2621) contains a 541-bp deletion in the promoter region leading to the deletion of two of the three LAG-1 binding sites.
source: We sequenced the lin-12 promoter in this allele and found a 541-bp deletion in the promoter region leading to the deletion of two of the three LAG-1 binding sites
evidence: DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Muscle arm development requires the positive transcriptional feedback of the LIN-12/Notch pathway.
source: Interestingly, the muscle arm development was similarly affected in lin-12(e2621), suggesting that the muscle arm development might require the positive transcriptional feedback of the LIN-12/Notch pathway.
evidence: Analysis of lin-12(e2621) phenotype shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: unc-40(e271) and madd-2(ok2226) mutants show missing or abnormal muscle arm phenotypes.
source: unc-40(e271) and madd-2(ok2226) show missing (middle) or abnormal (right) muscle arm phenotypes
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: UNC-40::GFP is preferentially expressed in vm2 and enriched on the muscle arms in wild type.
source: Note that UNC-40::GFP is preferentially expressed in vm2 and enriched on the muscle arms in the wild type
evidence: Expression analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: UNC-40::GFP is down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: Note that UNC-40::GFP is preferentially expressed in vm2 and enriched on the muscle arms in the wild type, and is down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant
evidence: Expression analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: MADD-2::GFP is preferentially expressed in vm2 in wild type and is down-regulated in the apx-1(wy755) mutant.
source: Note that MADD-2::GFP is preferentially expressed in vm2 in the wild type, and is down-regulated in the apx-1 (wy755) mutant
evidence: Expression analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: lin-12 is required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
source: The expression of both UNC-40 and MADD-2 in vm2 was significantly down-regulated in the lin-12(wy750) mutant, supporting the idea that lin-12 was required for the expression of unc-40 and madd-2 in vm2.
evidence: Expression analysis of translational reporters in mutant backgrounds

claim: Both unc-40 and madd-2 are preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells.
source: Both unc-40 and madd-2 were preferentially transcribed in vm2 cells
evidence: Transcriptional reporter analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The transcriptional activities of both unc-40 and madd-2 promoters are dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: the transcriptional activities of both promoters were dramatically suppressed in the lin-12(wy750) mutant
evidence: Transcriptional reporter analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The canonical LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway acts to promote the transcriptions of both unc-40 and madd-2 directly.
source: These data indicate that the canonical LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway acts to promote the transcriptions of both unc-40 and madd-2 directly.
evidence: Transcriptional reporter data and presence of LAG-1 binding sites

claim: Two LAG-1 consensus binding sites are found on the proximal promoter region of the madd-2 gene.
source: Consistent with this model, two LAG-1 consensus binding sites were found on the proximal promoter region of the madd-2 gene.
evidence: Sequence analysis of madd-2 promoter

claim: Two LAG-1 binding sites are found in the third intron of unc-40 that is essential for its expression.
source: Although no LAG-1 binding site was found in unc-40 promoter region, two were found in the third intron of unc-40 that is essential for its expression
evidence: Sequence analysis and personal communication with Daniel Colon-Ramos

claim: Forced expression of UNC-40 in vm2 from the unc-103e promoter induces the formation of muscle arms in the lin-12(wy750) mutant.
source: Note that the forced expression of UNC-40 in vm2 from the unc-103e promoter induces the formation of muscle arms in the lin-12(wy750) mutant
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Ectopic expression of UNC-40 in vm1 induces muscle arm-like membrane extensions.
source: Note that the ectopic expression of UNC-40 in vm1 induces the muscle arm-like membrane extensions
evidence: Ectopic expression experiment data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Misexpression of UNC-40 is sufficient to induce dendritic spine-like membrane extensions from vm1 cells.
source: We found that misexpression of UNC-40 was sufficient to induce the dendritic spine-like membrane extensions from vm1 cells
evidence: Ectopic expression experiment data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The vm1 muscle arms always form from the medial surface of vm1, the identical location as for the normal vm2 muscle arms.
source: Although the ectopic membrane extension from vm1 was usually thinner than the wild-type vm2 muscle arm, the vm1 muscle arms always formed from the medial surface of vm1, the identical location as for the normal vm2 muscle arms
evidence: Observation from ectopic expression experiments

claim: UNC-40 responds to specific environmental cues to guide the formation of muscle arms.
source: the vm1 muscle arms always formed from the medial surface of vm1, the identical location as for the normal vm2 muscle arms, suggesting that UNC-40 responds to specific environmental cues to guide the formation of muscle arms
evidence: Observation that ectopic UNC-40 induces muscle arms at stereotyped locations

claim: unc-40(n324); madd-2(ok2226) double mutants show slightly enhanced muscle arm defects compared to single mutants.
source: We generated an unc-40(n324); madd-2(ok2226) double mutant and found slightly enhanced muscle arm defects in the double mutants
evidence: Double mutant analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Overexpression of madd-2 partially rescues the muscle arm defects of unc-40(n324) null mutant.
source: We also found that the overexpression of madd-2 partially rescued the muscle arm defects of unc-40(n324) null mutant
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Overexpression of unc-40 largely rescues the muscle arm defects of madd-2(ok2226) mutant.
source: Conversely, overexpression of unc-40 largely rescued the muscle arm defects of madd-2(ok2226) mutant
evidence: Rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7C

claim: madd-2 likely functions synergistically with unc-40 to promote muscle arm formation.
source: overexpression of unc-40 largely rescued the muscle arm defects of madd-2(ok2226) mutant, suggesting that madd-2 likely functioned synergistically with unc-40 to promote muscle arm formation
evidence: Rescue experiment data and genetic interaction analysis

claim: Expression of madd-2 and unc-40 is not mutually regulated.
source: Expression of madd-2 and unc-40 is not mutually regulated
evidence: Expression analysis in mutant backgrounds shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: unc-40 and madd-2 at least partly function in parallel.
source: Expression of madd-2 and unc-40 is not mutually regulated, consistent to the hypothesis that unc-40 and madd-2 at least partly function in parallel
evidence: Expression analysis and genetic interaction data

claim: The postsynaptic development and synaptic target selection in the egg-laying circuit are mediated by the LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway.
source: We conclude that the postsynaptic development and synaptic target selection in the egg-laying circuit are mediated by the LIN-12/Notch signaling pathway.
evidence: Integration of all genetic, expression, and functional data

claim: The LIN-12/Notch pathway promotes the expression of UNC-40/DCC and MADD-2, which cooperate with each other to generate postsynaptic muscle arms.
source: The LIN-12/Notch pathway promotes the expression of UNC-40/DCC and MADD-2, which cooperates with each other to generate postsynaptic muscle arms.
evidence: Integration of expression, rescue, and genetic interaction data

claim: The vm2 muscle arm structure is functionally relevant postsynaptic specializations.
source: We found that both the postsynaptic potassium channel UNC-103E and a neurotransmitter receptor SER-1B were enriched on vm2 muscle arms, further supporting that the muscle arm structure is functionally relevant postsynaptic specializations
evidence: Expression data showing enrichment of postsynaptic markers on muscle arms

claim: The vm2 muscle arm is necessary for the integrated functional synapse.
source: In addition, the mutants lacking vm2 muscle arms show significant defects in the synchronized activation of vm2 and egg-laying behavior, indicating the necessity of the vm2 muscle arm for the integrated functional synapse.
evidence: Ca2+ imaging and behavioral data from mutants

claim: The ability to form muscle arms during development dictates the choice of vm2, but not its sister cell vm1, to become the postsynaptic partner of the egg-laying motor neurons.
source: Therefore, the ability to form muscle arms during development dictates the choice of vm2, but not its sister cell vm1, to become the postsynaptic partner of the egg-laying motor neurons.
evidence: Integration of anatomical, functional, and genetic data

claim: LIN-12/Notch signaling instructs both vulval organogenesis and synaptic development of the egg-laying circuit by regulating at least three sequential but independent developmental processes.
source: Therefore, we conclude that LIN-12/Notch signal instructs both vulval organogenesis and synaptic development of the egg-laying circuit by regulating at least three sequential but independent developmental processes: the AC/VU decision, in which LIN-12/Notch signaling promotes the differentiation of AC and VU cells; VPC specification, in which it determines the vulval precursor cell fates; and vm2 postsynaptic specification, in which it specifies the postsynaptic target cell and further regulates the muscle arm development.
evidence: Integration of developmental timing experiments and known roles of LIN-12

claim: Vulval morphogenesis requires a low level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activation, while vm2 postsynaptic specification requires a relatively high level of LIN-12/Notch activity.
source: Together, these data strongly argue that vulval morphogenesis requires a low level of LIN-12/Notch signaling activation, while vm2 postsynaptic specification requires a relatively high level of LIN-12/Notch activity.
evidence: Analysis of partial vs complete loss-of-function alleles and their differential effects

claim: vm2 muscle arm development involves a unilateral induction of LIN-12/Notch signaling activated by APX-1.
source: However, in vm2 muscle arm development, the lin-12 expression is down-regulated in the apx-1(wy755) mutant, while the apx-1 expression does not change in the lin-12(wy750) mutant. These results indicate a different unilateral induction of LIN-12/Notch signaling activated by APX-1.
evidence: Expression analysis in mutant backgrounds

claim: Vulval epithelial cells might provide a membrane-associated or locally secreted cue to guide the vm2 muscle arm extension.
source: These observations suggest that vulval epithelial cells might provide a membrane-associated or locally secreted cue to guide the vm2 muscle arm extension.
evidence: Observations of muscle arm phenotypes in egl-15 mutants with displaced vulval muscles

claim: unc-40, potentiated by madd-2, plays a deterministic role in guiding the muscle arm extension and the postsynaptic target selection.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that unc-40, potentiated by madd-2, plays a deterministic role in guiding the muscle arm extension and the postsynaptic target selection.
evidence: Integration of genetic, rescue, and ectopic expression data

claim: The formation of pre- and postsynaptic specializations can occur at different times in the egg-laying circuit.
source: First, the formation of pre- and postsynaptic specializations can occur at different times. The HSN presynaptic specializations form at the early L4 stage, significantly before the maturation of the postsynaptic targets. The extension of the postsynaptic muscle arms takes place 5–6 hr later.
evidence: Developmental timing observations

claim: The development of the pre- and postsynaptic specializations appears to be independent of each other in the egg-laying circuit.
source: Second, the development of the pre- and postsynaptic specializations appears to be independent of each other. Eliminating the postsynaptic cells does not affect the timing and location of synaptic vesicle accumulation in HSN neurons. Similarly, ablation of the presynaptic neurons has no obvious effect on the timing and direction of the muscle arm growth
evidence: Cell ablation experiments and mutant analysis

claim: Pre- and postsynaptic differentiations are guided by two different but related guidepost cells in the egg-laying circuit.
source: Third, pre- and postsynaptic differentiations are guided by two different but related guidepost cells.
evidence: Integration of current findings with previous work on HSN presynaptic development

claim: Primary vulval epithelial cells serve as guidepost cells for the HSN presynaptic development.
source: Through genetic analysis, we previously found that the primary vulval epithelial cells serve as guidepost cells for the HSN presynaptic development
evidence: Previous genetic studies cited in the manuscript

claim: Postsynaptic differentiation is likely guided by the secondary vulval epithelial cells.
source: Interestingly, postsynaptic differentiation is likely guided by the secondary vulval epithelial cells
evidence: Expression pattern of APX-1 and location of muscle arms relative to epithelial cells

claim: The muscle arms appear to grow along the interface between the primary and the secondary vulval epithelial cells through possibly an UNC-40-dependent mechanism.
source: The muscle arms appear to grow along the interface between the primary and the secondary vulval epithelial cells through possibly an UNC-40-dependent mechanism, which ensures that the pre- and postsynaptic compartments will contact each other.
evidence: Anatomical observations and UNC-40 function data

claim: The epithelial cells play organizational roles for the development of the entire vulval organ, coordinating multiple events including vulval muscle migration, axon guidance of HSN, VC axon branching and synapse formation.
source: The epithelial cells not only function as the channel for egg-laying but also play organizational roles for the development of the entire vulval organ, coordinating multiple events including vulval muscle migration, axon guidance of HSN, VC axon branching and synapse formation.
evidence: Integration of current findings with previous work on vulval development
